title: Why Are There Rocks Under Railway Tracks?
description:
Look under almost any railway track in the world and you will see the same thing. Rocks. Millions of sharp, gray stones, piled under and around the rails. They look like leftovers from construction, but they are one of the most carefully designed parts of the railway. Without them, a track would sink, flood, and twist out of shape in a few months. Today, ten parts of a railway track, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:19 1. The rocks
2:42 2. The sleepers
4:10 3. The rail clip
5:33 4. The rail's shape
6:54 5. The tamping machine
8:15 6. The stone washing machine
9:33 7. The extra rails on bridges
10:50 8. The box that counts axles
12:11 9. The yellow box between the rails
13:34 10. The heat detector
15:02 The verdict

Sources:
- Track ballast (functions, angular stone, depth, fouling): Wikipedia, "Track ballast" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_ballast
- Network Rail, "Track" (ballast, sleepers, rails) https://www.networkrail.co.uk/running-the-railway/looking-after-the-railway/track/
- Railroad ties (wood, creosote, concrete, composite): Wikipedia, "Railroad tie" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad_tie and Railway Tie Association, "FAQ" https://www.rta.org/faqs-main
- Pandrol clip (Per Pande-Rolfsen, 1957): Wikipedia, "Pandrol" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandrol
- Flat-bottomed rail (Vignoles 1836, Stevens 1830) and rail weights: Wikipedia, "Rail profile" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_profile
- Tamping machines and Plasser & Theurer: Wikipedia, "Tamping machine" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamping_machine
- Ballast cleaning and mud pumping: Wikipedia, "Ballast cleaner" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballast_cleaner
- Guard rails and catch points: Wikipedia, "Guard rail (rail)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guard_rail_(rail) and "Catch points" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catch_points
- Track circuits (William Robinson, 1872) and axle counters: Wikipedia, "Track circuit" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_circuit and "Axle counter" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axle_counter
- Eurobalise and ETCS: Wikipedia, "Eurobalise" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurobalise
- Hot box detectors: Wikipedia, "Hot box detector" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_box_detector
